probed.proposedFix: In scripts/v3/lib/axe-surface.js, add 'aria-roledescription' to the AXE_SURFACED_RULES set (the aria-validity 4.1.2 block, alongside aria-prohibited-attr at line 38). axe force-enables this rule in eval-page.js:284 and its selector [aria-roledescription] + supportedRoles gate fires a VIOLATION only when the attribute sits on a role that does not support it — exactly the kb1m8s failure. Once surfaced, build-v3's existing axeObs loop promotes the decided 4.1.2 violation to a PROVISIONAL BARRIER via AXE_SC_FAMILY['4.1.2']='name-role-value', flipping noObligation to a flagged barrier (requires the axe target to resolve to a real /-prefixed xpath via the data-v3-xp injection, which holds for this single div).
probed.effectivenessCritique: This would actually flip THIS case: the only blocker is the one-line allow-list omission; the promotion machinery and SC family mapping already exist and already handle aria-prohibited-attr identically. Over-fire risk is low and bounded: axe's aria-roledescription rule is gated by supportedRoles, so it fires as a violation ONLY on genuinely-prohibited usage (a generic/structural element), aligning with ACT kb1m8s; on the 3 Passed / 1 Inapplicable kb1m8s cases axe passes or doesn't match (correct usage on a supported role, or a different global prop). One real residual risk I could not fully close: build-v3.js:308 requires the axe target to resolve to a real DOM xpath (xpath[0]==='/'); axe returned a CSS target ["div"] in my standalone probe, and only the in-harness data-v3-xp injection upgrades it — if that element was not in the v3 collected element set the finding would still drop. For this single-div page it resolves, but on real pages the fix is only as good as the xpath resolution. Worth doing: it is a precise, low-cost, low-regression closure of a proven silent-miss FN that the prior round fixed with the wrong ruleId; it also picks up the analogous aria-roledescription-on-generic limb generally without opening wholesale 4.1.2.

probed.actRuleIntent: ACT afw4f7 "Text has minimum contrast": every text run must meet WCAG 1.4.3 (4.5:1 normal). This is Failed Example 7 — gray text rgba(90,90,90,0.8) spans a hard split gradient (transparent->black at 3.3em via linear-gradient), so with padding 0 1em the latter half of "Hello world" renders gray-on-black at ~2.30:1, a genuine failure (the white-half part is ~4.23:1, also sub-4.5).
probed.whyStillWrong: Genuine barrier the harness missed. The deterministic worst-case-barrier path (exp-runners.js lines 372-373) is gated on `a.foregroundResolved && a.backgroundResolved && a.fgColor`. This fixture has NO opaque DOM background-color: the span's bg is the transparent gradient, html/body backgroundColor is rgba(0,0,0,0), and the visible white is the browser's default CANVAS — not a DOM property. resolveAt() (line 109) only accepts a DOM backgroundColor with `a===1`, so baseEl=null -> bg=null -> backgroundResolved=false, and fgColor (line 184, guarded by backgroundResolved) is also null. The worst-case promotion is therefore doubly blocked. The runner dead-ends to INCONCLUSIVE (trace line 17: "The deterministic signal says the backdrop couldn't be reduced to [two colors]"), routes to contrast-over-complex-backdrop-v0, and the LLM false-clears: "uniformly light/white background across its entire run" (line 22). The rca-run4 trace shows the model even SAW the black region behind "world" and still cleared on perceptual legibility ("text remains clearly legible... NOT REPRODUCED"), confirming the rubric lane judges legibility, not the 2.30:1 WCAG ratio.
probed.proposedFix: In scripts/v3/lib/exp-runners.js measureContrast(): add a white-canvas fallback so that when resolveAt finds no opaque DOM base AND no foreign/pseudo painter intersects the ink rect, treat the effective base as rgb(255,255,255) (the browser default canvas), setting backgroundResolved=true with bg=white. Then in runTextContrastPixel()'s worst-case-barrier block (lines 372-383), for a translucent CSS fg recomposite the RAW fg (rgba 90,90,90,0.8) over each analyzeBackdrop candidate pixel (p05/p95/mean) before computing contrast, rather than using a single pre-composited a.fgColor — so worstContrast composites gray over the darkest rendered pixel (black) -> 2.30:1 <= 4.5-0.5 -> thresholdFailed=true -> deterministic barrier. The !pixelUniform + pixelAgrees gates remain, so this only fires on a genuinely non-uniform rendered backdrop and only promotes a clear FAIL.
probed.effectivenessCritique: Verified numerically it flips THIS case: worstContrast(gray-over-black, black)=2.30 <= 4.0 -> thresholdFailed, deterministic barrier, no longer routed to the false-clearing rubric. The white-canvas fallback is the standard assumption of every real contrast tool and is cross-checked by the existing pixelAgrees ±16 tolerance, so a wrong white assumption that disagrees with rendered pixels still abstains rather than false-clears. The worst-case path already requires !pixelUniform and a >=0.5 fail margin and never relaxes a CLEAR, so over-fire risk is low. The one real subtlety/risk is the translucent-fg recompositing: it must use the RAW rgba fg over each candidate pixel, not the pre-composited a.fgColor (which is null here) — implemented carelessly it could double-composite or mis-handle opaque fgs; needs the experiments.test.js afw4f7-analog test plus a new case for the transparent-canvas variant to guard regressions. Net: well-scoped, sound, and it fixes a whole class of "transparent background over default white canvas" 1.4.3 FNs, not just this one. Worth doing.

probed.rule: 7d6734 — SVG element with explicit role has non-empty accessible name
probed.actRuleIntent: Rule 7d6734 is applicable to any SVG element that has an EXPLICIT graphics/img role; it PASSES when that element has a non-empty accessible name. In this fixture the role-bearing element is the child <circle role="graphics-symbol" aria-label="1 circle">, which has a valid non-empty name — hence "Passed Example 2" / GT-passed. The bare parent <svg> has no role and is not the rule's target.
probed.whyStillWrong: The harness enumerates and judges the WRONG element. The collector's isImage (act-page-collect.js:245: `tag === 'svg'`) tags the bare parent <svg> as a graphic; that <svg> has no aria-label/role so its computed accessible name is empty. The oracle then mints a non-text-content (1.1.1) obligation on it (applicability-oracle.js:185: `el.isImage === true && el.removedFromA11yTree !== true`). The LLM rubric, handed the empty-named /html/body/svg[1], correctly-given-its-input returns "REPRODUCED ... has an empty accessible name." But the semantics live on the child <circle role="graphics-symbol" aria-label="1 circle">, which is properly named — this is W3C's deliberate PASS. Nothing special-cases graphics-symbol/graphics-document (grep: zero hits), so a roleless container <svg> whose content is carried by a named graphics-role descendant is mis-flagged.
probed.proposedFix: In act-page-collect.js, when computing the <svg> graphic record, detect that the SVG itself has no explicit role/own name but contains a descendant with an explicit graphics role (role^=graphics- or role=img) AND a non-empty accessible name (aria-label/aria-labelledby/title), and set a fact like svgNameOnDescendant=true (mirroring the existing svgLiveText carve-out at :248). Then in applicability-oracle.js:185 gate the non-text-content/images-of-text enumeration so a bare roleless <svg> with svgNameOnDescendant===true is NOT enumerated (its name obligation is satisfied by the named child). Lane: collector + applicability-oracle.
probed.effectivenessCritique: This WOULD flip THIS case: the obligation is minted solely on isImage+empty-name with no descendant awareness, so suppressing it removes the only in-scope verdict and the FP. The gate is narrow (requires an EXPLICIT graphics role AND a real non-empty name on a descendant), so regression risk is low — it matches exactly the W3C-blessed pattern and won't suppress a genuinely empty/unlabeled SVG (those have no named graphics-role child). Mild residual risk: if a single <svg> legitimately renders MULTIPLE informative graphics and only one child is named, the carve-out could under-flag — but that is an edge ACT 7d6734 itself treats per-role-element, and the alt-adequacy lane is non-authoritative anyway. The squeeze is modest (one mis-modeled SVG family) but the fix is principled (the collector currently flattens every <svg> to a single atomic image, ignoring descendant semantics) and parallels the existing svgLiveText precedent, so it is worth doing. Confidence medium because I'm inferring the W3C pass intent from the fixture without re-running the deterministic probe; the screenshot would only re-confirm the empty SVG name, not the applicability error.

probed.actRuleIntent: An SVG element with an explicit role (here role="graphics-document") must have a non-empty accessible name; this fixture is a PASSED example because the SVG's first-child <title>1 circle</title> element supplies the accessible name "1 circle".
probed.whyStillWrong: The collector computes the SVG accessible name from the title ATTRIBUTE only, never the SVG child <title> ELEMENT. In act-page-collect.js the name terms are el.getAttribute('title') (line 161-162, 270, and _accName line 322) plus alt/aria-label — for <svg><title>1 circle</title>...</svg> getAttribute('title') is null, so axName collapses to "". That empty name is what fed the rubric: the trace premises "The accessible name is empty (no alt/label)" (line 16) and the verdict says it "has an empty accessible name" (line 8). The one tool that could have corrected it — query_ax_node — failed: TOOL_RESULT "node not found at the given xpath/coordinate" (line 24) and capture_full_page returned "target not found" (line 26), because cdp-tools.js line 40 resolves the xpath with document.evaluate('/html/body/svg[1]') which does not match an SVG-namespace element under a null-namespace path. So the model fell back on the wrong frozen evidence and REPRODUCED. The SVG's true accName is "1 circle"; the page genuinely PASSES 1.1.1.
probed.proposedFix: In scripts/v3/lib/act-page-collect.js, include the SVG first-child <title> element text in the accessible-name terms. Add an svg-title term, e.g. const svgTitle = tag === 'svg' ? ((el.querySelector(':scope > title') || {}).textContent || '') : ''; and fold it into _accName (line 322) and authorName (line 270), and into the interactive-path bits (around line 161-162) for svg. This makes the SVG report axName="1 circle", so the alt-text-adequacy rubric is no longer handed "empty accessible name" and clears the obligation. Secondarily (defense in depth, not load-bearing) cdp-tools.js line 40 should resolve namespaced SVG xpath steps (e.g. via local-name() or a namespace resolver) so query_ax_node can verify the SVG node instead of returning "not found".
probed.effectivenessCritique: The collector fix is the load-bearing one and would almost certainly flip THIS case: the rubric's REPRODUCED hinges entirely on the injected "empty accessible name" premise, so supplying axName="1 circle" removes the barrier signal and the obligation clears (no second pixel-mismatch issue here — the title text "1 circle" matches a single rendered circle). Risk/over-fire is low and bounded: SVG <title> as a direct child is the spec-defined name source, so reading it only ADDS correct names; it will not fabricate names for SVGs that lack a <title>. Watch two edge cases: (1) only the FIRST direct-child <title> names the SVG (use :scope > title and take the first), and an aria-label/aria-labelledby must still WIN over <title> per accname precedence — the existing author-name-wins ordering already handles aria-label, so append svgTitle as a lower-priority term; (2) <title> deeper inside the SVG names a sub-shape, not the root SVG, so :scope > (direct child) is essential to avoid pulling nested titles. The CDP xpath-namespace fix is worth doing for the broader SVG cluster (it would let the LLM self-correct future SVG cases) but is NOT needed to fix this case and is lower priority. Net: worth doing — small, spec-correct, and it kills a real FP plus likely sibling SVG-with-title cases.

probed.actRuleIntent: A focusable element must not trap keyboard focus: 80af7b Failed Example 3 is a mutual-bounce trap where btn1/btn2 re-grab each other's focus on blur (onblur="moveFocusToButton(...)" with trapOn=true), confining focus to {btn1,btn2} so link2 is unreachable and only the non-standard Ctrl+M exits — a genuine 2.1.2 barrier.
probed.whyStillWrong: The trap IS a real barrier (correct FN) and the deterministic confinement detector confirms it — my isolated probe returned deterministicTrapConfirmed:true with members {button[1],button[2]} 5/5 times. But run5 scored noObligation: results.json shows inScopeObligations:2, inScopeAutoPartial:0, agentVerdicts:[], outcome:"noObligation". Root cause: detectFixedSetConfinementTraps anchors the finding to a SINGLE element (kbd-graph.js line 381 `const anchor = members[0]` = [...S][0] = button[2]); run-instruments.js line 78 emits only `xpath: t.xpath`, discarding `memberXpaths`. build-v3 §5b (line 427 `if (deterministicIds.has(o.obligationId)) continue`) only fills an obligation with NO deterministic disposition. The C5 keyboard-trap-escape experiment (exp-runners.js:871), which cannot see the async bounce, returns a non-authoritative PARTIAL that lands button[2] in `partials`→deterministicIds, BLOCKING the trap fill on the very element the finding anchors to. My repro: 3/4 raw runs gave button[2]:PARTIAL(deterministic) → trap dropped → noObligation; siblings 9/11 only got caught because their anchor element happened to stay auto-PARTIAL.
probed.proposedFix: Two-part. (1) run-instruments.js line 78: fan the confinement finding out over EVERY member — `(confine.traps||[]).flatMap(t => (t.memberXpaths?.length ? [...new Set(t.memberXpaths)] : [t.xpath]).map(xp => ({sc:t.sc, kind:'keyboard-trap', detector:'confinement', xpath:xp, detail:...})))` — so the barrier can land on whichever member's obligation is still auto-PARTIAL. I verified this flips case-8 from 0→9/10 caught. (2) For full robustness, narrow build-v3 §5b so a CONFIRMED keyboard-trap obs (kind keyboard-trap/-self-refocus, ~0-FP by construction) is allowed to UPGRADE an INCONCLUSIVE experiment PARTIAL on the SAME 2.1.2 obligation (treat the C5 keyboard-trap-escape "trapProven:false, escape unproven" PARTIAL as abstaining, not authoritative) — this covers the residual 1/10 where BOTH members took an experiment PARTIAL simultaneously.
probed.effectivenessCritique: Part (1) is verified to ACTUALLY move this case (0→9/10 caught over 10 orchestrate repeats) — it is not just plausible; the member-fanout is low-risk because the confinement detector is sound-by-construction (escape-route guard, >=3 focusables, Esc check) so emitting on each member of an ALREADY-confirmed trap cannot over-fire — it only spreads a barrier that is genuinely true for every confined member. Regression surface is tiny: it touches one map() in the instrument lane for the confinement detector only; legit modals/passed-bounce examples never produce a confirmed confinement finding, so nothing new fires there. The one real caveat: part (1) alone is flaky-mitigating, not flaky-eliminating (1/10 residual when both members race to an experiment PARTIAL), so the deeper part (2) — letting a confirmed trap dominate an inconclusive experiment PARTIAL — is what makes it deterministic; that change is more delicate (must scope strictly to INCONCLUSIVE 2.1.2 keyboard-trap-escape PARTIALs to avoid overriding a real escape-proven clear), but the kbd-trap detectors are the harness's most adversarially-hardened lane, so the risk is acceptable. Worth doing: this is the harness's own coverage gap (the detector found the trap and the pipeline threw it away), affecting the whole 80af7b Failed-3/4/5 family, not a GT-granularity artifact.

probed.rule: 80af7b Focusable element has no keyboard trap
probed.actRuleIntent: Whether keyboard focus can be moved away from a focusable element using standard navigation (Tab/Shift+Tab) without a documented non-standard escape; this fixture (Failed Example 4) is a mutual-bounce trap: btn1.onblur refocuses btn2 and vice versa while trapOn=true, so Tab/Shift+Tab never leaves the {btn1,btn2} set, and the only escape is the undocumented non-standard Ctrl+M — a genuine 2.1.2 trap.
probed.whyStillWrong: The trap is REAL and the detector CATCHES it: my live puppeteer probe of detectFixedSetConfinementTraps on the fixture returned deterministicTrapConfirmed:true for the confined set memberXpaths=[/html/body/button[2],/html/body/button[1]]. But the signal never reaches the score. Three compounding defects: (1) run-instruments.js:78 emits the confinement finding with only the ANCHOR xpath (/html/body/button[2]), dropping t.memberXpaths so button[1] (the GT-scored subject) gets no obligation; (2) build-v3.js:283 promotes it as source:'instrument' and shadowObservations (line 658) excludes trapObs; (3) orchestrator.js:196 derives the LLM's deterministicTrapConfirmed only from built.results.shadowObservations filtered on source==='deterministic' — which can NEVER match an 'instrument'-sourced trap (only the escape EXPERIMENT is source:'deterministic', and per build-v3.js:269 it ABSTAINS on async/refocus traps). So the LLM saw 'keyboardTrapContext.deterministicTrapConfirmed:false / inTrapRiskRegion:true' (the bare focusRisk heuristic from the inline onfocus/onblur) and correctly stayed PARTIAL: "the deterministic walk could not verify whether Tab/Shift+Tab/Esc successfully moves focus away." The §5b fill (build-v3.js:421) filled only button[2]'s obligation, leaving button[1] at auto-PARTIAL → outcome uncertain → FN.
probed.proposedFix: collector lane. In run-instruments.js:78, emit one keyboard-trap finding per member xpath of a confinement trap (iterate t.memberXpaths || [t.xpath]) instead of only the anchor t.xpath, so build-v3.js:276-285 mints a trapObs (source:'instrument', BARRIER_OBSERVED) for EACH confined element including /html/body/button[1]; the existing §5b fill (build-v3.js:421, which already consumes trapObs by obligation-xpath) then fills button[1]'s auto-PARTIAL with a PROVISIONAL BARRIER, flipping the case to a 2.1.2 barrier independent of the LLM. Secondary (helps the LLM lane, not required to flip score): in orchestrator.js:195-197, also accept source==='instrument' keyboard-trap observations when deriving trapBarrierXpaths (and include them, e.g. read from built.results trapObs), so the agent receives deterministicTrapConfirmed:true.
probed.effectivenessCritique: This WOULD flip the case, not just sound plausible: I confirmed by live probe that the confinement detector already returns deterministicTrapConfirmed:true with button[1] in memberXpaths, and the §5b fill path (build-v3.js:421) already keys obligations by xpath and consumes trapObs — the ONLY missing link is that line 78 discards memberXpaths, so button[1] never gets a trapObs. Emitting per-member trapObs lands a PROVISIONAL BARRIER on button[1]'s exact obligation. Regression risk is low: the detector is documented sound-by-construction with 0 false positives across all 80af7b passed/inapplicable examples, and memberXpaths are precisely the elements proven confined (Tab+Shift+Tab+Escape all fail), so filling each member's obligation is no less sound than filling the anchor's — it cannot over-fire beyond what the anchor fill already asserts. The orchestrator source-filter fix is a real latent bug too (deterministicTrapConfirmed is dead for confinement+self-refocus traps), worth doing for the LLM lane's correctness, but it is secondary because the per-member fill alone flips the score. Net: worth doing, small surgical collector change with a clear deterministic basis.

probed.rule: 7d6734 SVG element with explicit role has non-empty accessible name
probed.actRuleIntent: An <svg> carrying an explicit role (here role="img") must have a non-empty accessible name. This fixture is a Passed Example: the SVG's name is supplied by its <title>1 circle</title> CHILD element (computed AX name "1 circle", role image, in-tree), so it satisfies 1.1.1. GT = PASSED.
probed.whyStillWrong: The xpath generator (act-page-collect.js:64-71 xpathOf) emits "/html/body/svg[1]" from the lowercased tagName. SVG lives in the SVG namespace, and a plain XPath step `svg` does NOT match a namespaced element, so document.evaluate('/html/body/svg[1]') returns null (empirically confirmed: plainSvg:null; svgNS:"http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"). This breaks BOTH resolvers: (1) the collector's authoritative CDP name pass at act-page-collect.js:478 (resolveAx) returns null -> "unresolved -> keep the heuristic axName", and the heuristic labelledText (lines 145-180) never reads SVG <title> CHILDREN, so axName stays ""; (2) the live query_ax_node tool at cdp-tools.js:40 returns the trace's line 27 result: {"resolved":false,"reason":"node not found at the given xpath/coordinate"}. The model was therefore fed "Accessible name: empty, not present" (trace lines 17-18) and its coordinate fallback hit role:none/inTree:false (trace line 38), so it ruled REPRODUCED on a false premise. Resolving the SAME node via querySelector/local-name() gives CDP AX name "1 circle", role image, ignored:false (empirically verified) -> the page genuinely PASSES.
probed.proposedFix: Add a namespace-agnostic xpath fallback at the two resolver sites that broke this case: act-page-collect.js:478 (resolveAx, the authoritative-name pass) and cdp-tools.js:40 (query_ax_node). When document.evaluate(plainXpath).singleNodeValue is null, retry once with each segment rewritten `/tag[n]` -> `/*[local-name()="tag"][n]` (applied per `>>`-split frame segment so cross-frame descent is preserved). Keep the generator (xpathOf) byte-identical so cross-lane join keys stay stable; only the resolution gains the fallback. Empirically verified: the rewritten xpath /*[local-name()="html"]/*[local-name()="body"]/*[local-name()="svg"][1] resolves the SVG and yields AX name "1 circle". This restores el.axName/el.inTree/el.cdpRole for the collector and resolved AX facts for the live tool, so the LLM sees the real name and the rubric clears the SVG.
probed.effectivenessCritique: High confidence this flips the case: with axName="1 circle" and inTree=true fed to the alt-text-adequacy rubric, the "empty name / not in tree" steer that drove REPRODUCED disappears, and query_ax_node would return resolved facts instead of resolved:false. Regression risk is low because the rewrite is a FALLBACK only when the plain evaluate returns null (never alters already-resolving HTML xpaths), and local-name()="div" matches HTML elements identically. Scope is meaningful, not a one-off: ~29 result files carry /svg[ xpaths, and no namespace handling exists anywhere today, so every SVG-dependent SC (1.1.1 SVG alt, 4.1.2 SVG role/name, SVG non-text contrast) is currently silently degraded to the heuristic that can't read SVG <title> children. Caveats: must apply the rewrite per `>>` segment (don't flatten frame descent), and the required-state live-read at cdp-tools.js:62 uses the same document.evaluate and would also need the fallback to be fully consistent (minor, not load-bearing for this case). MathML elements get the same benefit for free. Worth doing.

probed.actRuleIntent: Whether a focusable element traps keyboard focus: here two buttons each set a global trapOn=true on focus and, on blur, call moveFocusToButton(other) which forces focus back to the sibling, so Tab/Shift+Tab cannot escape; the documented "Press Ctrl+M to Exit" handler (escapeTrapOnCtrlM) is NEVER registered, so per ACT this is a genuine, non-escapable keyboard trap (Failed Example 5).
probed.whyStillWrong: The asserted trap does NOT reproduce in the harness's engine. I ran the real deterministic detectors and a focus-event probe in headless Chromium (the harness's engine, page-lease.js:24 puppeteer.launch). Forward sweep settled cleanly: link1,btn1,btn2,link2,BODY,link1,... and Shift+Tab btn2->btn1->link1->... — focus escapes BOTH directions with trapOn=true at every step. The decisive line: "after Tab off btn2 (toward link2), active= link2" with focusin log=["focusin:link2"] — btn1 never receives focusin. Chromium ignores the .focus() call made inside the onblur handler because the in-progress Tab navigation has already committed, so moveFocusToButton never retains focus. detectFixedSetConfinementTraps/detectKeyboardTraps/detectFocusRetentionTraps all returned traps:[]. The harness therefore correctly observed no trap, surfaced only inTrapRiskRegion:true (inline focus handler present), and the LLM, told "flag a barrier ONLY if you can confirm focus cannot be moved away" (llm-adjudicator.js:245), honestly returned PARTIAL. GT says fail because the ACT author's expectation assumes a browser (historically IE/Firefox) where focus()-during-blur wins.
probed.proposedFix: none
probed.effectivenessCritique: The only way to "flip" this to a confirmed barrier is either (a) a static-pattern detector that flags "onblur calls a focus-mover gated on an onfocus-set flag, with no registered escape keydown handler," or (b) feeding the LLM the inline-handler source plus the dead "Ctrl+M" instruction. Both are unjustified. (a) is brittle idiom-matching on this single fixture's pattern and would over-fire on legitimate focus-management modals that DO release focus or DO register an escape handler — exactly the false-positive guard the existing escEscapes/close-control checks were built to prevent. (b) would have the LLM assert a trap the live engine demonstrably does NOT exhibit — i.e. override empirical observation with code-reading speculation, which contradicts the harness's "absence in the engine is the truth" stance and the rubric's explicit "confirm focus cannot be moved away" gate. My own probe proves a real keyboard user in Chromium is NOT trapped here, so flagging would be asserting a barrier that does not exist in the rendering engine the dataset is captured in. PARTIAL is the honest verdict; this FN is a GT/engine-granularity artifact (ACT's manual expectation vs. Chromium behavior), not a harness defect. Leave it alone.

probed.actRuleIntent: kb1m8s tests that ARIA *global* states/properties are not authored on an element whose role prohibits them (ARIA 1.2 §5.2.5 prohibited states/properties). The fixture `<h1 role="none" aria-brailleroledescription="Banana text">` applies role=none (presentation) which strips semantics and PROHIBITS the global property aria-brailleroledescription — GT=failed is canonical, scored under 4.1.2 (name-role-value).
probed.whyStillWrong: Genuine barrier, missed. run4 was noObligation; the run5 fix (e61b378) let it reach the LLM but via the WRONG signal/rubric. Real axe-core 4.12.1 on this fixture fires `presentation-role-conflict` as a VIOLATION (tags best-practice/ACT, no wcag tag) and `aria-braille-equivalent` only as INCOMPLETE (wcag2a/wcag412). The harness maps presentation-role-conflict to 1.1.1 review:true (axe-surface.js:67) so it never touches 4.1.2; and the AXE-PROMOTION lane only promotes `kind==='violation'` (build-v3.js:305 `if (... f.kind !== 'violation' ...) continue`), so the wcag412-tagged braille finding — being INCOMPLETE — falls through to the CHECKER-UNCERTAINTY lane, mints a 4.1.2 `name-role-value` obligation, and routes to `accessible-name-adequacy-v0`. The LLM then cleared it: its `query_ax_node` returned `role:"heading", inTree:true` (the browser resolved the role-none conflict in favor of the heading), so it concluded "no aria-labelledby, no aria-describedby, no prohibited ARIA attributes surfaced... the live measurement wins" — never inspecting the AUTHORED `aria-brailleroledescription` on `role="none"`, because the tool surfaces only the resolved AX node, not authored attributes, and the rubric's ARIA-legality branch is gated on a `aria-prohibited-attr` checkerHint that was not present.
probed.proposedFix: Add a deterministic ARIA-validity detector in build-v3.js (alongside the dangling-idref/ax-name-presence signals over `bundle.collect.elements`): when an element's AUTHORED role is `none`/`presentation` AND it carries any global ARIA state/property (aria-label, aria-roledescription, aria-braillelabel, aria-brailleroledescription, aria-describedby, aria-details, aria-keyshortcuts, etc.), emit a 4.1.2 `name-role-value` deterministic barrier (authoritative:false, shadow) and MINT its obligation — mirroring the existing AXE-DECIDED obligation-minting at build-v3.js:375. This requires collect.elements to expose authored attributes (role + the aria-* keys); if it already does, the detector is a few lines; if not, add the small attribute snapshot to vsr-collect/eval-page. Do NOT re-map axe's broad `presentation-role-conflict` wholesale to 4.1.2 (it fires on benign layout role=presentation with no aria-*).
probed.effectivenessCritique:
It WOULD flip this case: role=none + aria-brailleroledescription is exactly the authored condition, deterministic and not LLM-dependent, so it sidesteps the false-clear entirely. It also generalizes to the noObligation siblings (case-4 `
` is a prohibited global on a bare div; case-3 `

` is role-specific not global, so it would NOT be caught by a *global*-only gate — that one stays an aria-prohibited-attr facet the oracle deliberately suppresses for flooding). Over-fire risk is the real concern: aria-roledescription/aria-describedby are common and legitimately allowed on most elements — the gate MUST be narrow (role=none/presentation specifically, where ALL globals are prohibited), not "any global aria anywhere," or it will spray FPs across normal pages. Given the gate is tight and the condition is a hard ARIA-spec fact, it is defensible. Caveat on yield: this rescues 1, maybe 2 of 3 kb1m8s FNs; the broader aria-prohibited-attr facet was suppressed on purpose for noise, so a full kb1m8s sweep is a larger precision/recall tradeoff. Worth doing as a tight, spec-anchored deterministic rule, not as a general aria-prohibited revival.

probed.actRuleIntent: Whether a link's purpose is descriptive from its accessible name plus its PROGRAMMATICALLY-DETERMINABLE context (enclosing sentence/paragraph/list-item/cell/own heading). Here the link "Workshop" sits alone in its own paragraph p[2], separate from the descriptive sentence in p[1].
probed.whyStillWrong:
The LLM hallucinated the context. Trace line 19: "the link sits inside the sentence 'The W3C held a [Workshop]', making 'Workshop' an enclosing-sentence context." That is false per the fixture: the descriptive sentence is in p[1] ("The W3C held a workshop on June 9-10, 2005..."), and the link is a STANDALONE paragraph p[2] (`

Workshop

`) whose only text is the single word "Workshop". This is the rule's canonical "Failed Example 4" — link name "Workshop" with no enclosing-sentence context fails 2.4.4. The model fabricated an enclosing sentence by merging the two sibling paragraphs, producing LIKELY_OK instead of REPRODUCED, so the GT-failed link was not flagged.
probed.proposedFix: Collector/rubric (link-purpose-v0): supply the LLM an explicit, structured "programmatically-determinable context" payload instead of a free-form region blob. For 5effbb/2.4.4 link-purpose, the context block should be the link's OWN enclosing block element only (the ancestor p/li/td/heading that directly contains the anchor) with sibling block boundaries marked, NOT a flattened neighborhood of adjacent paragraphs. The rubric prompt should state: "Adjacent sibling paragraphs are NOT enclosing context. If the link is the sole content of its block, its determinable context is empty." Here that yields context="Workshop" (own p has no other text), forcing REPRODUCED.
probed.effectivenessCritique:
This would flip THIS case only if the context payload genuinely stops merging p[1] into p[2]; the root cause is the model conflating two sibling

elements it saw in a shared "surrounding region" blob, so the fix must change WHAT the collector feeds, not just nag in the prompt — a prompt-only caution is fragile and may not flip it. Risk: ACT's "context" for 2.4.4 legitimately can include the enclosing paragraph/list; over-narrowing to "own block only" would create FPs on genuine Passed examples where the link IS inside a descriptive sentence (e.g. inline "

Read the workshop report for details

") — but those cases keep the link inside the same block so own-block scoping still captures them correctly. The real over-fire risk is cases where ACT counts a list-item's sibling context or a preceding heading; the fix must keep headings/li/td/caption as valid context and exclude only adjacent sibling paragraphs. Net: worth doing because the failure mode (hallucinated enclosing sentence from a flattened blob) is a recurring, principled defect for link-purpose, and the block-scoped context is well-defined; but it is a collector-payload change, not a one-line prompt tweak, and needs a regression check against Passed inline-link examples.

probed.actRuleIntent: ACT 047fe0 "Document has heading for non-repeated content" (mapped to 2.4.10 via H69) tests whether the non-repeated/main content of the document is introduced by at least one heading that is exposed in the accessibility tree. Here the only heading over #main is <h1 aria-hidden="true">, so the non-repeated content has NO accessible heading — a definitive failure (this is the rule's own "Failed Example 3", expected=failed).
probed.whyStillWrong: The fixture genuinely fails: #main's sole heading is aria-hidden, so for AT users the chapter content is unheaded. The model had the decisive signal — it noted "ariaHidden: true — this heading is removed from the accessibility tree" three times in the trace — but then returned N/A via the verdict line: "the page contains only one substantive content section ... so the 2.4.10 multi-section precondition is not met and the criterion does not apply." Root cause is a rubric-instruction conflict in section-headings-v0.md: the "PRECONDITION — multiple sections (apply this FIRST)" block (lines 49-53) tells the model to return N/A for any single-section page "even if it has no heading at all," and that veto pre-empted the rubric's own correct aria-hidden path (lines 26-28: aria-hidden heading → section UNHEADED → REPRODUCED). The multi-section gate (faithful to true WCAG 2.4.10 AAA) is wrong for ACT 047fe0, which requires only a single accessible heading for the non-repeated content.
probed.proposedFix: Edit scripts/v3/llm-rubrics/section-headings-v0.md: scope the multi-section precondition so it does NOT veto the heading-absence case. After "even if it has no heading at all," add an explicit carve-out: a single-section page is N/A ONLY when its content is introduced by a real a11y-tree heading OR genuinely owes none; but if the page DOES ship an h1-h6/role=heading over the main content and that heading is removed from the a11y tree (ariaHidden:true in structure.headings[]) or is visual-only/off-document, then the non-repeated content is UNHEADED → REPRODUCED, regardless of section count. I.e. make the lines 26-28 aria-hidden rule take precedence over the multi-section precondition when an aria-hidden heading exists over the main content. The collector already carries the needed fact (act-page-collect.js:445 sets ariaHidden per heading), so no collector change is required.
probed.effectivenessCritique: This should actually flip the case: the model already surfaced ariaHidden:true and only chose N/A because the precondition told it to; removing that veto for the aria-hidden-heading-present case routes it to REPRODUCED, the correct GT-failed answer. Regression risk is the real question. The 9 passing 047fe0 examples include legitimate single-section pages — the fix must fire ONLY when an actual heading element exists over the main content but is aria-hidden/visual-only, not when a page simply has one well-formed heading or genuinely needs none. Because the carve-out keys on a concrete observable fact (a heading present in structure.headings[] with ariaHidden:true, or visually-hidden/off-document), it is narrow and should not over-fire on the passing single-heading examples. Residual caveat: this is the known WCAG-2.4.10-vs-ACT-047fe0 semantic divergence (HARDCODED-JUDGMENTS audit territory) — the rubric was deliberately WCAG-AAA-faithful (multi-section), so a heavy-handed rewrite could break true-2.4.10 single-topic passes elsewhere; keep the edit surgical (aria-hidden/visual-only-heading-present only) and re-run the full 047fe0 set (esp. the single-section passes) to confirm specificity. Worth doing: the fix is low-cost, targets a clear instruction bug, and the data is already present — the lane fills non-authoritatively so risk to authoritative verdicts is nil.

probed.actRuleIntent: Whether two+ links with identical accessible names in the SAME programmatic context resolve to the same/equivalent resources — OR, per the third expectation clause + SC 2.4.4's "ambiguous to users in general" exception, whether the destinations are equally indeterminate to ALL users (so the disabled user is not disadvantaged). PASSES when links serve equivalent purpose OR are ambiguous-to-everyone; FAILS only when context disambiguates differing destinations for some-but-not-all users.
probed.whyStillWrong: GT is "Passed Example 9" (expected:"passed") — its rationale: identical name "ACT rules" + different resources, BUT "the purpose of these links is ambiguous to users in general...the person with a disability is not at any disadvantage." The saved fixture's prose "We are on social media:" triggers this exception. The model applied the rubric's 3rd failure mode literally: trace line 23 "This is the classic 2.4.4 failure mode: identical names, different destinations" → LIKELY_BARRIER. The rubric link-purpose-v0.md (lines 44-48, 57-59) defines "Identical names, DIFFERENT purpose ⇒ barrier" with ZERO mention of the "ambiguous to users in general" exception, so the deterministic distinctRawHrefs=2 signal + origin resolution deterministically produced the flag. The fixture has the discriminating text in hand but the rubric has no rule that could PASS on it.
probed.proposedFix: none (the only safe change is marginal): in link-purpose-v0.md add an "ambiguous-to-users-in-general" guard to the identical-names failure mode — when the surrounding context frames BOTH same-named links as generic equivalent pointers (e.g. "We are on social media: X, X") such that no reader (sighted or not) can tell the destinations apart, return PARTIAL instead of REPRODUCED rather than asserting a barrier. Do NOT teach it to PASS, because the discriminator vs Failed Example 2 ("W3C pages for ACT:"/"Community group for ACT:", byte-identical hrefs/names) is too fine to adjudicate reliably.
probed.effectivenessCritique: Be skeptical: this is the worst possible discrimination in the corpus. Passed Example 9 (228c0a3d, this case) and Failed Example 2 (8dc58c48) have IDENTICAL hrefs and IDENTICAL accessible names — both are present in the corpus — and differ ONLY by surrounding prose ("social media:" → PASS vs "W3C pages for ACT:"/"Community group" → FAIL). Any rubric edit that teaches the ambiguity exception strongly enough to flip THIS case to non-barrier risks flipping Failed Example 2 into a false NEGATIVE — trading a specificity miss for a recall miss, which is the worse error for this harness. The PARTIAL guard is the only defensible move (it stops asserting a barrier without claiming a pass), but PARTIAL still does not score as GT-passed, so it does NOT actually flip the FP per ACT per-SC granularity — it just makes the verdict honest. The harness's LIKELY_BARRIER is the mainline practical reading; ACT calls it PASS only via a narrow SC exception. Net: not worth a behavioral fix; the case is genuine honest-uncertainty where PARTIAL is the right answer and the rule authors themselves flag it as borderline (Passed 9 fails the stricter 2.4.9).

probed.actRuleIntent: Two links with identical accessible names in the same context must resolve to the same OR equivalent resources; if same name + same context but the links lead to different/non-equivalent destinations, the rule FAILS (link purpose ambiguous).
probed.whyStillWrong: The GT label is "failed" because the canonical W3C "Failed Example 1" uses two "contact us" links with DIFFERENT query strings — verified on w3.org: `contact-us.html?page=1` (Chat) vs `contact-us.html?page=2` (Call) — which render different content, so identical names point to non-equivalent destinations. But the SAVED fixture (pages/fd3a94/9ceacbea...html) has BOTH hrefs as bare `contact-us.html` with NO query string (grep shows two byte-identical `contact-us.html`). The query strings that constitute the violation were stripped during corpus capture. On the saved bytes, the harness reasoning is CORRECT: the model called `resolve_destination`, got byte-equal fingerprints for both links ("finalUrl ...contact-us.html, title 'About - Chat with us', h1 'Chat With Us'" — identical), and concluded "Both 'contact us' links share the same accessible name and resolve to the same destination, so there is no 2.4.4 failure." Same name + same context + same destination = equivalent purpose = genuinely PASSES. The FN is entirely an artifact of the saved fixture no longer containing the distinguishing `?page=1`/`?page=2`.
probed.proposedFix: none
probed.effectivenessCritique: No harness change can or should flip this case. The two saved hrefs are byte-identical (`contact-us.html` == `contact-us.html`); both resolve_destination fingerprints are byte-equal. Any rule that flagged this would have to flag two truly-identical-href links as a 2.4.4 failure, which is wrong by the rule's own definition (same resource = equivalent purpose = pass) and would over-fire massively on every legitimate page that repeats the same link twice (extremely common: duplicate "Home"/"Read more"/"contact us" links to one URL). The harness here is not just defensibly right, it is correctly reasoning over the evidence it has and even did the right diligence (resolved destinations rather than trusting raw hrefs per the rubric's "absence != pass" caution). The defect is upstream in corpus capture: the page-saver dropped the `?page=N` query strings (likely query-string normalization or a single-file snapshot that didn't preserve per-link params). The only real fix is to RE-CAPTURE this fixture preserving the query strings, or exclude fd3a94 Failed Example 1 from the FN denominator as a known-corrupted fixture — neither is a harness-lane change. Not worth any runner/rubric work; leave the verdict as-is and flag the fixture for re-capture.

probed.actRuleIntent: fd3a94 flags a SET of links that have matching accessible names AND the same programmatic link context but resolve to a DIFFERENT purpose/destination. It fails when same-named/same-context links go somewhere meaningfully different; it passes when they go to an equivalent destination.
probed.whyStillWrong: The SAVED fixture is corrupted relative to upstream. Upstream W3C (verified via WebFetch of the live testcase) has two links: href=".../contact-us.html?page=1" (reveals the "Chat With Us" section) and ".../contact-us.html?page=2" (reveals "Call Us") — genuinely different purposes, so GT="failed" is correct. But the saved page (eval/checker-comparison/act-subset/pages/fd3a94/ef75d42424140b163d7939aacc6a80c8dbc8816a.html, lines 5-6) had the ?page query strings stripped at capture: `grep -o ... | uniq -c` shows BOTH hrefs are byte-identical "...contact-us.html" (count 2). Given that input, resolve_destination correctly returned byte-equal fingerprints, and the LLM correctly reasoned "Both 'Contact Us' links resolve to the identical settled URL ... every fingerprint field is byte-equal" → NOT REPRODUCED / LIKELY_OK. The harness, CDP tool, rubric and LLM all did the right thing on the data they were given; the discriminating evidence was destroyed before run time.
probed.proposedFix: none (at the harness/run-time level). The only real fix is in the corpus-capture/mirroring lane: re-download fd3a94 testcase ef75d424... from upstream preserving the ?page=1 / ?page=2 query strings on the two anchors (and audit the mirror tool for query-string stripping on .html links generally). No change to the runner, CDP resolve_destination tool, link-purpose-v0 rubric, or LLM would recover the lost params.
probed.effectivenessCritique: Be skeptical: no run-time change CAN flip this case, because the evidence (?page=1 vs ?page=2) is absent from the saved bytes — the two anchors are literally identical strings, no <base>, no redirect. Any rubric/LLM tweak that "flagged it anyway" would be flagging on no evidence and would over-fire on legitimate PASS cases where same-named links truly share a destination (9 of 17 fd3a94 cases are passed/inapplicable). The collector re-capture IS the correct and only effective fix, but it is corpus hygiene, not a defect in the probed harness logic, and it touches exactly one fixture (low corpus-wide yield) though it may indicate a class bug in query-string preservation worth a one-time audit. For the run5 harness as probed, leave it alone — the verdict is the only defensible answer for the saved input.

probed.actRuleIntent: For an in-context link, the accessible name PLUS its programmatically-determined enclosing context (the closest p ancestor) must convey the link's purpose. Fixture is W3C "Passed Example 3": link text "this product" inside the sentence "See the description of this product." pointing to an on-page anchor #desc whose paragraph reads "This product consists of several web pages." — the WG deems this purpose determinable (PASS/inapplicable-as-barrier).
probed.whyStillWrong: The model gathered the right context (OCR returned the full enclosing paragraph "See the description of this product.") but applied an over-strict standard: it concluded "the sentence restates the pronoun ('this product') but never names [the specific product]" and fired the rubric's "Generic-in-context" failure mode. It never credited that the enclosing sentence states the link's FUNCTION ("See the description …") and the link is an in-page anchor (href="#desc") to that description — so the purpose ("go to the description of this product") IS resolved by name+context. Verdict line: "RUBRIC 2.4.4 LIKELY_BARRIER … a generic pronoun reference whose enclosing sentence … never identifies which product, leaving the link's destination indeterminate." The link's destination is not indeterminate; it is the on-page description, which is exactly what 2.4.4 requires.
probed.proposedFix: none
probed.effectivenessCritique: A rubric tweak COULD flip this case: add a passed-example calibration that an enclosing sentence stating the link's function relative to an on-page/anchor destination ("See the description of …") resolves purpose even when the link text is a pronoun. But this is the wrong trade. The rubric was deliberately hardened (lines 26-35, 43) against exactly the "context restates the topic but never resolves the destination" false-clear, and "See the description of this product" sits on the razor's edge between that hardening and the W3C PASS. Any phrasing permissive enough to clear this will tend to also clear borderline FAILs like "Read more about this product"/"See details of this product," re-opening the corpus FPs the hardening was built to catch. 2.4.4 is genuinely soft and this is essentially the only 2.4.4 case in scope — one specificity miss on a known-ambiguous W3C example is not worth regressing the format-list/Read-more recall. The model's reasoning is WCAG-defensible on a strict reading (a pronoun link is weak); it is scored wrong only because ACT labels this borderline construction a PASS. Better left alone.

probed.actRuleIntent: fd3a94 (QW-ACT-R44) checks that two-or-more links with IDENTICAL accessible names in the SAME context resolve to the same or equivalent resources; the "Contact us" block here (chat + phone icons over two "Contact Us" links) is the rule's Failed Example where the icons promise distinct contact methods (chat vs phone) yet, in the ORIGINAL page, the two same-named links lead to different resources.
probed.whyStillWrong: The decisive fact is in the saved bytes, not the model: both anchors have byte-identical href ".../contact-us.html" — no query string, no fragment, no onclick, no data-attr (verified: HREFS identical=True, any query/fragment=False). The TOOL_RESULT confirms both resolve to the SAME finalUrl/title "About - Chat with us"/h1, "all equality fields true", so the model's NOT REPRODUCED / LIKELY_OK verdict ("Both 'Contact Us' links resolve to the identical settled destination") is the only defensible reading of the fixture as it exists. GT is "failed" because the ORIGINAL upstream page distinguished the two destinations via query strings (e.g. ?page=1/?page=2) that were STRIPPED at fixture-capture time; the discriminating signal is permanently gone from the saved bytes. The harness's own RUN4 RCA already tagged exactly this case `no-gt-artifact`: "the query string was stripped at capture, so both hrefs resolve identically ... fixable: No — re-capture only."
probed.proposedFix: none
probed.effectivenessCritique: No harness change can flip this case correctly. The two saved hrefs are byte-identical, so any rubric/oracle/tool that flagged a 2.4.4 barrier here would be flagging on NO evidence — it would have to invent a difference that the fixture does not contain, and that same heuristic would then over-fire on every legitimately-passing same-name/same-destination pair (e.g. fd3a94/7ebe961d, which the docs note is correctly cleared). Run5's round actually fixed the right things (SVG-ns xpath, sibling surfacing, resolve_destination wiring) and the model used the tool exactly as intended; the tool faithfully reported byte-equality of identical URLs, which only made the by-GT-wrong answer MORE confident — correct tool behavior on a corrupted fixture. The only real "fix" is collector-side: re-capture the fixture preserving href query strings (RUN4 RCA's prescribed capture-side fix). But that is re-acquiring the corpus, not a harness-logic change, and is out of scope for the frozen dataset. Leave it: the verdict is the right answer to the question the saved bytes pose; the FN is a pure GT-vs-corrupted-fixture mismatch. Not worth chasing within the frozen corpus.

probed.actRuleIntent: Two-or-more links INCLUDED IN THE ACCESSIBILITY TREE that share the same accessible name in the same context must resolve to equivalent destinations/purpose; a same-named link removed from the a11y tree is not an applicable subject.
probed.whyStillWrong: The fixture's second link is `ACT rules` — REMOVED from the a11y tree, so fd3a94 sees only ONE applicable "ACT rules" link and is INAPPLICABLE (GT passed). The harness still flagged a barrier because `selectRubricSubjects` builds the same-name index (llm-adjudicator.js:631-639) over every link-role element with a non-empty name, and at line 635 falls back to `el.text` ('ACT rules') when `el.axName` is the (correctly) resolved-empty string for the aria-hidden node — re-introducing it as a same-name peer. The trace's deterministic signal then reports two same-named links with distinctRawHrefs=2, and the rubric concludes 'Two links sharing the identical accessible name ACT rules resolve to different destinations ... a clear 2.4.4 barrier.' The index never consults `el.removedFromA11yTree`/`el.inTree`, both already set on the record (act-page-collect.js:268,492) and used elsewhere in the same file (llm-adjudicator.js:301-302).
probed.proposedFix: In scripts/v3/lib/llm-adjudicator.js, in the `linksByName` index loop (~line 632-639) add a guard that skips a11y-tree-removed links: `if (el.removedFromA11yTree === true || el.inTree === false) continue;` (place after the role check). Optionally mirror the same exclusion in `sameNameLinksFor` for symmetry. This makes the aria-hidden 'ACT rules' link stop counting as a 2.4.4 same-name peer, matching fd3a94 applicability (links must be in the accessibility tree). Add a regression fixture to scripts/v3/tests/item14a-linkset.test.js: an aria-hidden same-named link must yield NO sameNameLinks signal.
probed.effectivenessCritique: This DOES flip the case: the LIKELY_BARRIER has exactly one trigger — the same-name peer carried in __sameNameLinks — because v3Barrier(deterministic)=false and the visible link's own name ('ACT rules' + 'social media' context) is not generic, so without the peer the rubric returns NOT REPRODUCED/PARTIAL, not a flag. The fix is principled and matches existing usage of inTree/removedFromA11yTree in this same file, so it carries near-zero regression risk: it only drops links AT users can never reach, which is precisely fd3a94's applicability condition. The one edge to watch is a CDP-resolution failure leaving inTree undefined, but removedFromA11yTree is purely attribute-driven for aria-hidden and reliable, so the guard still fires. Note this contradicts the prior RC1 log (RC1-RUBRIC-ITERATION-LOG.md:140) that filed fd3a94/9abd9bcf as 'irreducible / harness-defensibly-right (same-page-fragment / residual ambiguity)' — that triage misread the fixture; it is the aria-hidden inapplicable variant, a genuine specificity bug, and the small filter is clearly worth doing because it generalizes to every aria-hidden same-named link.

probed.actRuleIntent: Two+ links sharing the same accessible name in the same programmatic context must resolve to the same or an equivalent resource (or be visually disambiguated when pointing to non-equivalent resources); identical-name links going to genuinely different destinations with no disambiguation FAIL.
probed.whyStillWrong: The GT label "failed" was inherited from the W3C source page (Failed Example 3: two "Contact Us" links to contact-us.html?page=1 [chat] vs ?page=2 [phone] — genuinely different rendered resources). But the SAVED fixture was corrupted during corpus capture: both hrefs are byte-identical `contact-us.html` with NO query parameter (`grep` shows "2 href=...contact-us.html", distinctRawHrefs=1, query-params=0), and the chat/phone icons are separated into a sibling span rather than CSS backgrounds on the links. The model did exactly the right thing — TOOL mcp__cdp__resolve_destination returned "same final URL, same title 'About - Chat with us', same H1 'Chat With Us'... All equality fields are true" — so LIKELY_OK is the only defensible verdict for the bytes on disk. The failure condition (different destinations) no longer exists in the artifact.
probed.proposedFix: none
probed.effectivenessCritique: No rubric/oracle/tool fix can flip this without fabricating evidence absent from the saved bytes. The capture stripped the `?page=1`/`?page=2` query strings that were the entire basis of the W3C failure, collapsing two-different-destinations into two-identical-destinations — and resolve_destination correctly confirms they're identical. Forcing a FAIL on same-name+same-href would be wrong on the merits and would over-fire on legitimate equivalent-link patterns (e.g. duplicate "Read more"→same article), tanking specificity. A sibling case (dddcd76a...) retained its query params, showing the loss is per-case corpus damage, not a systemic re-capture target worth chasing for one case. The only "fix" is at the dataset layer (re-scrape preserving query strings or drop the broken fixture from GT), not in the harness lanes. Leave the harness verdict; it is right about the artifact it can see. Score it as a GT/capture artifact, not a recall miss.

probed.actRuleIntent: Two+ links with identical accessible names in the same context must resolve to the same/equivalent resource; here two SVG <a> elements both named "Contact Us" must point to equivalent destinations or the page fails 2.4.4.
probed.whyStillWrong: The saved fixture is corrupted: the canonical W3C "Failed Example 7" (rule page line 909/918) has the two links pointing to contact-us.html?page=1 and contact-us.html?page=2 (different resources → genuine fail). But the mirrored fixture stripped the query strings — both hrefs are now byte-identical "../_assets/.../contact-us.html" (confirmed: grep for "?page" = 0 matches; both hrefs identical). The model correctly read distinctRawHrefs:1 and concluded "the sole same-named peer resolves to the same destination" → LIKELY_OK. That verdict is CORRECT for the bytes given; the discriminating evidence (differing ?page= query strings) was destroyed at mirror time. A sibling fixture dddcd76a (same rule, onclick= form) kept its ?page=1/?page=2 because the rewriter only touched href/src attributes, proving the stripping happened in the href-relativizer.
probed.proposedFix: none (for this saved fixture as-is). The only real remedy is upstream in the mirror/collector lane: when relativizing href/src attributes, preserve the query string and fragment (do not drop "?page=1"). Re-mirroring fd3a94/7ebe961dbb4f from the stored worklist url would restore the two distinct hrefs and the LLM would then see distinctRawHrefs:2 and flag it. But against the current saved bytes no harness change can recover the lost query strings.
probed.effectivenessCritique: A rubric/oracle change would NOT flip this case and would be actively harmful: there is no signal in the saved fixture distinguishing the two byte-identical hrefs, so any rule that flags it would be flagging on the bare existence of same-named peers — which is exactly the over-fire the rule's "equivalent purpose" exception is designed to avoid, and would create FPs on every legitimate duplicate-link page (the rule's passing examples). The model behaved correctly. The genuine fix is the collector preserving query strings during href relativization, which would help this and any other query-string-discriminated case (4.1.2/2.4.4 link sets), but it requires re-mirroring the corpus, not a code path the run5 verdict can use. For THIS scored case it is best left as a known GT-vs-saved-fixture artifact; the harness is defensibly right on the bytes. Worth filing the collector query-string-preservation note in DEFERRED-TODO, but not worth touching the judge.

probed.actRuleIntent: 307n5z tests that elements with presentational children (button/checkbox/img/etc.) have NO descendants in sequential focus navigation — a structural focus problem, NOT accessible-name adequacy. Here ``: the anchor has no href so it is not focusable, so the presentational child is non-focusable → genuine PASS (the fixture is literally "Passed Example 4").
probed.whyStillWrong: Two stacked errors. (1) The applicability oracle mints a 4.1.2 `name-role-value` obligation for the `<button>` purely because it matches WIDGET_ROLE (applicability-oracle.js:67,136) and routes it to accessible-name-adequacy-v0 — testing a DIFFERENT 4.1.2 facet (name quality) than 307n5z tests (focusable presentational children). (2) The rubric verdict is itself wrong: trace line 7-8 / SAY block declares "The button's accessible name 'button/link' is a content-free placeholder naming the element's type/role category." But "button/link" is a real human-readable string and is NOT in the rubric's NARROW reserved-keyword set (lines 24-30: only `{{name}}`, `%LABEL%`, literal markup, or bare `undefined/null/aria-label/label/role`). The rubric explicitly PASSES "a name that merely restates the control's type — INCLUDING a multi-word phrase that mentions the control type." The model overfit "names the element type" into "placeholder," violating its own rubric. Because GT is per-SC, any flag on 4.1.2 scores FP against this passed example.
probed.proposedFix: Reinforce accessible-name-adequacy-v0.md's placeholder clause so the narrow reserved set is unmistakable: add an explicit NOT-a-placeholder example for role/type-restating strings, e.g. add to the PASS list "a name that is one or more control-type words ('button/link', 'button', 'link', 'menu') PASSES — restating the control type is adequate for 4.1.2; only an un-substituted template token or a bare single reserved keyword fails." Optionally tighten the placeholder predicate to a literal closed set (a deterministic pre-check in the rubric harness that only the listed reserved keywords / `{{...}}`/`%...%`/`<...>` markup count as placeholders) so a slash-joined real-word string can never be classified as content-free.
probed.effectivenessCritique: Skeptical read: the rubric ALREADY says exactly the right thing — a name that "merely restates the control's type" PASSES — so this is a model-adherence miss, not a missing instruction. Adding the literal "button/link" example would likely flip THIS case (the model latched onto the surface pattern "names the type/category"), but text-reinforcement of an instruction the model already had is a soft fix with no guarantee across reruns; it may also nudge the model to under-flag genuine `{{token}}` placeholders if over-broadened. The deterministic placeholder-predicate variant is the durable fix and would hard-flip this and similar cases without LLM variance, but it adds machinery for a narrow failure mode. The deeper structural issue (the oracle minting a name-adequacy obligation for a 307n5z fixture that only tests focusable presentational children) is not curable here without a 307n5z-specific check, and that facet legitimately exists on real pages — so I would NOT try to suppress the 4.1.2 obligation. Net: the rubric text/predicate fix is worth doing because the model verdict is plainly wrong on its own terms (it contradicts the rubric), it is low-risk if scoped to the reserved-keyword closed set, and it generalizes to other generic-but-real names. Marginal-to-yes; the deterministic-closed-set variant is the one actually worth shipping.

probed.actRuleIntent: Two links with the identical accessible name "Contact Us" in the same context must serve equivalent purpose; here they navigate (via onclick) to contact-us.html?page=1 (renders "Chat With Us") vs ?page=2 (renders "Call Us") — different purposes, so 2.4.4 FAILS.
probed.whyStillWrong: The destination divergence lives ONLY in the onclick attribute (location='.../contact-us.html?page=1' vs '?page=2'), which neither the deterministic same-name-link index nor resolve_destination reads. The same-name collector takes el.href (act-page-collect.js L229/L356 + llm-adjudicator.js L638); spans have no href → distinctRawHrefs:0, wrongly signaling "no distinct raw hrefs". resolve_destination (cdp-tools.js L614-616) only follows a.href and returned the decisive line: {"error":"no href on the target"}, resolvedCount:0. The model's run5 verdict therefore reads: "destination cannot be verified (no href; resolve_destination failed), so a same-name/different-destination barrier cannot be ruled out" → UNCERTAIN, which is scored as a recall miss (manifest outcome:"uncertain"). GT = "Failed Example 6" = failed, so this is a genuine FN. (Note: run4 worsened it — observe_state_after_activation navigated both onclick targets to the SAME offline 404 page because the absolute /WAI/... path isn't mirrored, falsely "confirming same destination".)
probed.proposedFix: Collector lane: in scripts/v3/lib/act-page-collect.js, when an element has no href but has an onclick/role=link, statically extract a navigation URL from the handler (regex for location=, location.href=, location.assign(, window.open( with a string literal) and store it as a jsHref fallback. Thread that into the same-name index (llm-adjudicator.js L638 href: el.href || el.jsHref) so distinctRawHrefs correctly becomes 2 for ?page=1 vs ?page=2. Mirror the same fallback in cdp-tools.js resolveOne (L614): if no a.href, read the element's onclick and resolve the static literal URL instead of returning "no href on the target". With distinctRawHrefs=2 surfaced and resolve_destination able to fingerprint the two different ?page targets, the rubric flips UNCERTAIN→a 2.4.4 fail.
probed.effectivenessCritique: This would actually flip the case: the two onclick literals differ only in ?page=1 vs ?page=2, a trivially parseable static difference, and once distinctRawHrefs=2 is surfaced (or resolve_destination fingerprints the two genuinely different rendered pages) the rubric has concrete different-destination evidence — strictly better than the offline-activation path which is an active trap here (both 404 to the same page). Skeptical caveats: (1) onclick parsing must be narrow — only string-literal navigations (location=/assign/window.open); handlers like onclick="doX()" yield no URL and must fall back to today's PARTIAL, not a false fail, so no over-fire on non-navigating spans. (2) Distinct raw hrefs alone shouldn't hard-fail — the rubric still correctly treats raw-href inequality as "could diverge but verify"; the real lift is making resolve_destination able to follow onclick so it can compare the SETTLED ?page=1 vs ?page=2 pages (which differ: Chat vs Call). (3) Scope is narrow (2.4.4 onclick-driven pseudo-links), so regression surface is small. Worth doing: this is a recurring ACT pattern (JS-driven role=link is common) and the fix removes a genuine recall blind spot, but only the resolve_destination onclick-follow half is load-bearing for flipping verdicts — the collector distinctRawHrefs half is mainly a better uncertainty signal.

probed.actRuleIntent: Whether a form field's programmatic label is DESCRIPTIVE of its purpose, judged on the VISIBLE label + visual context. Here a search input's aria-labelledby="submit search" assembles its accessible name from a visible "Go" button and a display:none "Search" span; only "Go" is visible, which is not descriptive of a search field (GT expected=failed, "Failed Example 5").
probed.whyStillWrong: GT=failed but run5 returned uncertain/PARTIAL (FN, recall miss). The decisive verdict line: "the exact assembled accessible name cannot be confirmed, leaving descriptiveness under 2.4.6 unresolved." Two root causes. (1) Evidence gap: query_ax_node's idrefStatus (cdp-tools.js:84) returns per-IDREF only {id, present, hasText} — NOT each token's visibility or resolved text. So the LLM saw labelledby:[{id:submit,present,hasText},{id:search,present,hasText}] and literally could not tell that "search" (the only descriptive token) is display:none nor that the texts are "Go"/"Search", forcing an honest abstain. (2) Rubric gap: heading-descriptive-v0 models reversed-order and generic labels but NOT the actual cc0f0a failure mode — a programmatic label token that is hidden contributes to the accessible name but NOT to VISIBLE descriptiveness, so only the visible "Go" counts and is non-descriptive. The LLM chased a "reversed order" hypothesis (its rubric's framing) instead of the visible-only test the rule applies.
probed.proposedFix: Primary (cdp-tool lane, scripts/v3/lib/cdp-tools.js idrefStatus ~line 84): enrich each aria-labelledby/describedby IDREF entry with `visible` (computed display/visibility/aria-hidden) and `text` (resolved textContent) so the entry becomes {id, present, hasText, text, visible}. Secondary (rubric lane, heading-descriptive-v0.md): add a clause — "a labelledby token that is display:none/visibility:hidden DOES feed the accessible name but is NOT VISIBLE; descriptiveness for 2.4.6 is judged on the VISIBLE label + visual context. If the only visible token is a generic action word (e.g. 'Go', 'Submit') on a free-text/search field while the descriptive token is hidden, the visible label is non-descriptive → REPRODUCED." Both are needed: the evidence change is load-bearing (the rubric cannot fire without per-token visibility).
probed.effectivenessCritique: Would it flip THIS case? Plausibly yes — with {id:search,text:"Search",visible:false}/{id:submit,text:"Go",visible:true} in hand plus the new clause, the model can conclude only "Go" is visible and reach REPRODUCED. But honest doubts: (a) the model already hedged on a borderline descriptiveness call; "Go Search" is not egregiously generic, so it may still PARTIAL even with full evidence. (b) This is a single contrived fixture (Failed Example 5); corpus yield is low. (c) Exposing resolved label text/visibility broadly risks other rubrics (field-label-v0, accessible-name-adequacy-v0, link-purpose-v0 all read labelledby) over-trusting author text or mis-weighting hidden tokens — a small specificity risk. The evidence enrichment itself is principled and low-regression (additive fields, mirrors accname/visibility semantics), so it's defensible regardless. Net: worth doing as a principled evidence fix, but flagged marginal because it may not reliably flip this borderline case and the corpus payoff is thin.
